title: In Luke 7 What Does The Faith Of The Centurion Teach Us About Understanding Authority In Relation To Jesus
paragraphs: The Faith of the Centurion: Understanding Authority in Relation to Jesus (Luke 7)

The account of the centurion's faith in Luke 7:1-10 presents one of the most profound encounters with Jesus in the Gospels. This Roman officer's extraordinary faith not only astonished Jesus but also offers vital lessons on the nature of true faith, humility, and the recognition of Jesus’ divine authority.
1. The Centurion’s Humility and Worthiness
The centurion, though a man of significant social and military standing, approaches Jesus with remarkable humility. He does not consider himself worthy for Jesus to enter his home:
for I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: wherefore neither thought I myself worthy to come unto thee: but say the word, and my servant shall be healed. - Luke 7:6-7 ASV

This humility is key in approaching Christ. The centurion recognizes his own unworthiness, echoing the biblical truth that salvation and blessing are the result of God’s grace, not our merit (Ephesians 2:8-9 ASV).
2. Understanding Authority: The Centurion’s Insight
The centurion explains his confidence in Jesus by referencing his own experience with authority:

For I also am a man set under authority, having under myself soldiers: and I say to this one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it. - Luke 7:8 ASV

He recognizes that just as his spoken command is obeyed by his subordinates, so Jesus’ word carries power over sickness and the physical world. This demonstrates a profound understanding that Jesus’ authority is not limited by proximity or ritual, but is absolute and divine.
This insight reflects the biblical teaching that Jesus possesses all authority:
And Jesus came to them and spake unto them, saying, All authority hath been given unto me in heaven and on earth. - Matthew 28:18 ASV
3. The Nature of True Faith
Jesus marvels at the centurion’s faith, declaring:
I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. - Luke 7:9 ASV

True faith is not merely intellectual assent, but trust in the person and authority of Jesus. The centurion believes that Jesus’ word alone is sufficient. This is the essence of biblical faith: trusting in Christ’s power, even when we cannot see the outcome (Hebrews 11:1 ASV).
4. Implications for Believers Today

Submission to Christ’s Authority: Just as the centurion recognized earthly and spiritual authority, believers are called to submit every area of life to Jesus, trusting His sovereignty and wisdom (Colossians 1:18 ASV).

Prayer and Expectation: The centurion’s faith challenges us to approach Jesus with confidence that He is able and willing to answer according to His will, even when we cannot see the solution (1 John 5:14 ASV).
Inclusivity of the Gospel: The centurion, a Gentile, is commended for his faith, pointing to the truth that salvation in Christ extends to all who believe (Romans 10:12 ASV).
Conclusion

The faith of the centurion in Luke 7 teaches us that understanding and submitting to the authority of Jesus is at the heart of true faith. It is not our status, background, or worthiness that commends us to Christ, but our trust in His word and His authority as Lord over all.
